chapters.title: Chapter 2: How Deals Get Done in India

lessons.title: Delistings and Squeeze-Outs: When a Company Leaves the Exchange

children.text: In 2020, Vedanta Resources tried to take its Indian subsidiary Vedanta Ltd private. It set an indicative price of ₹87.50 per share. The stock had already risen on the news, many public shareholders placed bids at prices far above the indicative price, and the offer failed in October 2020 because not enough shares were tendered to cross the required threshold. Shareholders who had bought expecting a delisting premium were left holding a still-listed stock and no exit. Delistings look like easy money. The rules explain why they often are not.

body.text: In a voluntary delisting, public shareholders collectively set the price, but only if enough of them agree to sell. The acquirer needs to reach 90%, and every bid you place is a vote on the price at which you are willing to leave. If the threshold is not met, the company stays listed and any delisting premium in the share price disappears.

children.text: You already met delisting through a merger: HDFC Ltd left the exchanges in 2023 because it merged into HDFC Bank. That route needs no price discovery because you receive listed shares instead of cash. The rest of this lesson focuses on cash exits, where you have to decide on a price.
How a Voluntary Delisting Works
The rules are in the SEBI (Delisting of Equity Shares) Regulations, 2021. The steps follow a strict order.
Initial announcement.
The acquirer announces its intention to delist, usually with an indicative price. A peer review company conducts due diligence and the board considers the proposal.
Shareholder approval.
A special resolution is passed by postal ballot or e-voting, and votes cast by public shareholders in favour must be at least two times the votes cast by public shareholders against.
Floor price.
Set by a formula similar to the open offer price you learned in Lesson 2.3, looking back at prices paid by the acquirer and market prices before the announcement.
Bidding window.
Public shareholders tender their shares through the stock exchange mechanism, each stating the price at which they are willing to sell. This process is called
reverse book building

markDefs.definition: A price discovery process where sellers, not buyers, submit bids. Shareholders tender shares at the prices they want, and the exit price is the price at which enough shares have been tendered for the acquirer to reach the required threshold.

children.text: Discovered price and decision.
The acquirer accepts the discovered price, rejects it, or in specified cases makes a counter-offer. If it accepts and the threshold is met, the shares are delisted.
Exit window.
Shareholders who did not tender can still sell to the acquirer at the final price for one year after delisting.

children.text: Worked Example: Discovering the Price for Nilgiri Bearings

Nilgiri Bearings, a fictional listed company, has 10 crore shares. Its foreign parent owns 75% and wants to delist it. The floor price is ₹500. Public shareholders hold 2.5 crore shares. To reach 90%, the parent needs 9 crore shares, so 1.5 crore public shares must be tendered.

body.latex: \text{Discovered price} = \text{lowest bid price at which } \frac{\text{Promoter shares} + \text{Shares tendered at or below that price}}{\text{Total shares}} \geq 90\%
body.caption: Bids are stacked from the lowest price upwards until the acquirer's holding crosses the threshold.
Nilgiri Bearings: bids received
headers: Parent's holding if accepted at this price

body.title: Parent's holding as bids stack up
Find the discovered price
body.prompt: Using the Nilgiri Bearings bid table, what is the discovered price in rupees?
body.explanation: At ₹550 the parent reaches only 87% (7.5 crore + 1.2 crore = 8.7 crore). At ₹600 it reaches 91% (7.5 crore + 1.6 crore = 9.1 crore), crossing 90% for the first time. So ₹600 is the discovered price, 20% above the ₹500 floor.

body.title: What happens to your bid?
body.question: The parent accepts the discovered price of ₹600. You bid 300 shares at ₹550. Your friend bid 300 shares at ₹650. What happens?
options: You get ₹550 per share and your friend gets ₹650 per share
Both of you get ₹600 per share for all 300 shares
You get ₹600 per share. Your friend's bid is not accepted and the shares are returned, but they can still sell at ₹600 during the exit window
Only your friend's bid is accepted, because it was the higher price
body.explanation: Every accepted share is bought at the single discovered price. Your bid at ₹550 was at or below ₹600, so you receive ₹600, more than you asked for. Your friend's bid at ₹650 was above the discovered price, so it is rejected. Once the company is delisted, your friend can still sell to the parent at ₹600 for one year through the exit window.

body.text: Bidding high is not free. If too many public shareholders bid well above what the acquirer will pay, the discovered price climbs too high or the threshold is never reached. The acquirer walks away and the stock usually falls back to where it traded before the delisting news. Collective greed is the most common way delistings fail.

body.label: Vedanta Ltd's failed delisting, October 2020
body.context: Valid tenders fell short of the number needed for Vedanta Resources to reach 90%, and many public shareholders had bid at prices well above the indicative price. Vedanta Ltd stayed listed.

body.title: Name the process
body.textWithBlank: In a voluntary delisting, the exit price is discovered through reverse book ___, where selling shareholders state the price at which they will tender.
body.explanation: Reverse book building flips an IPO book: instead of buyers bidding to buy, existing shareholders bid to sell, and the acquirer's required threshold sets the price.

children.text: Compulsory Delisting: The Penalty Version

columns.label: Voluntary delisting
points: Initiated by the promoter or acquirer
Needs public shareholder approval by a 2 : 1 majority
Price discovered through reverse book building or offered at a fixed premium
Usually a healthy company whose owner wants full control
Company can relist only after a cooling-off period of five years

columns.label: Compulsory delisting
points: Imposed by the stock exchange for serious non-compliance, such as prolonged suspension
Fair value set by an independent valuer appointed by the exchange
Promoters must buy shares from public shareholders at that fair value
Company, promoters and directors are barred from the securities market, and the company cannot relist for ten years

body.text: A compulsory delisting on paper protects you, because promoters must buy you out at fair value. In practice, the companies delisted this way are often shell companies or firms whose promoters have vanished, and recovering that value can be slow or impossible. Treat trading suspensions and repeated non-compliance notices from the exchange as serious red flags long before delisting arrives.

body.title: Squeeze-outs: what happens to the last few shareholders

children.text: After a delisting, a small number of shareholders often remain. India has no simple, automatic squeeze-out, but there are two main routes.
Section 236 of the Companies Act, 2013.

A person or group holding 90% or more of a company's equity can notify the company of its intention to buy the remaining shares, at a price determined by a registered valuer. Minority shareholders can also offer their shares to the majority.
Reduction of share capital under Section 66.
The company cancels the minority's shares and pays them out, with shareholder approval by special resolution and NCLT confirmation. The tribunal examines whether the price is fair.

If you hold shares in a delisted company, you can usually still sell to the acquirer during the one-year exit window. After that, selling unlisted shares becomes much harder, so do not ignore the exit window letters.

body.title: Buying on the delisting headline
body.scenario: A fictional MNC subsidiary, Coromandel Filters, trades at ₹1,000. Its foreign parent, holding 80%, announces plans to delist it at an indicative price of ₹1,050. The next morning the stock opens at ₹1,180. A friend tells you to buy because "delisting prices always end up way higher than the indicative price, maybe ₹1,500".
body.prompt: Should you buy at ₹1,180 to bid in the delisting? Weigh the upside and the downside.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Upside: if the discovered price is ₹1,500 and the parent accepts, you make ₹320 per share, about 27% on ₹1,180.
2. Downside: if the parent rejects the discovered price or the threshold is not met, the stock is likely to fall back towards its pre-announcement level of about ₹1,000, a loss of around ₹180 per share, or 15%.
3. Threshold maths: the parent holds 80% and needs 90%, so it needs half of the 20% public float to tender. If a large chunk of shares sits with retail investors who do not participate, reaching 90% can be hard.
4. The acquirer's walk-away point: ₹1,050 is what the parent wants to pay, and nothing forces it to accept ₹1,500. Vedanta in 2020 shows that discovered prices far above the indicative price can simply be rejected.
5. Time: approvals, the vote and the bidding window take months, during which your money is tied up.
6. Conclusion: this is a bet on a specific event, not an investment in the business. If you do it, size it small and decide in advance what bid price you would genuinely be happy to exit at.

body.title: If a stock you own announces a delisting
steps: Note the acquirer's current holding and how many public shares it needs to reach 90%
Check the indicative price, the floor price and whether it is a reverse book building or fixed price offer
Vote in the special resolution: only public shareholder votes decide it
Bid at a price you would genuinely be happy to exit at, not a hopeful number
If your bid is rejected or you did not tender, use the one-year exit window
If the offer fails, expect the price to fall back and decide whether you still want to own the stock

body.label: BSE India
body.description: BSE publishes delisting notices, reverse book building results and lists of compulsorily delisted companies in its corporates section.

cards.definition: Removal of a company's shares from the exchanges at the request of its promoter or acquirer, under the SEBI Delisting Regulations, 2021.
Price discovery where public shareholders bid the prices at which they will sell, and the price at which the acquirer reaches 90% becomes the discovered price.
The minimum price for a delisting offer, set by a formula based on past acquisition and market prices.
The price at which cumulative tendered shares take the acquirer's holding to the required threshold.
The one-year period after delisting during which remaining shareholders can sell to the acquirer at the final price.
Delisting imposed by a stock exchange as a penalty, with promoters required to buy out public shareholders at fair value.
Buying out the last minority shareholders, in India mainly through Section 236 or a capital reduction under Section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013.

points: Companies leave the exchange through voluntary delisting, a merger, compulsory delisting, or a squeeze-out of remaining minority shareholders.
A voluntary delisting needs public shareholders' votes in favour to be at least twice those against, and the acquirer must reach 90% after the offer.
In reverse book building, the discovered price is the lowest price at which the acquirer crosses 90%, and every accepted share gets that single price.
The acquirer can reject the discovered price, as Vedanta's failed 2020 delisting showed, and the stock then usually gives up its delisting premium.
Shareholders who do not tender, or whose bids are too high, can still sell at the final price during the one-year exit window.
Compulsory delisting is a penalty and usually signals deep governance problems, not a payday.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, tax or legal advice. Nilgiri Bearings, Coromandel Filters and the investors in the examples are fictional. The regulatory thresholds and processes are simplified summaries of the SEBI (Delisting of Equity Shares) Regulations, 2021 as amended and the Companies Act, 2013, and individual offers can involve additional conditions. Always read the letter of offer and bid form before tendering.
